facts.fact_text: On 4 July 2002 the applicant organised a demonstration aimed at forcing the authorities to preserve the ballot papers of the 2002 legislative elections with a view to a potential recounting.

The demonstration organised by the applicant on 4 July 2002 consisted of completely blocking all six lanes of Erzsébet Bridge, a centrally situated bridge over the Danube, by parking six cars across it with their doors locked.
The demonstration on 4 July 2002 started at about 8.20 a.m.
The demonstrators, including the applicant, refused to comply with the police's order to remove the vehicles and leave Erzsébet Bridge.
At about 11.00 a.m. on 4 July 2002 the cars blocking Erzsébet Bridge were finally towed away by the police.
Traffic flow on Erzsébet Bridge resumed at about 12 noon on 4 July 2002.
On 5 July 2002 the Pest Central District Court imposed a regulatory fine of 50,000 Hungarian forints on the applicant.

On 2 September 2002 the Budapest XI District Police Department fined the applicant for a parking offence consisting of his parking his car in the middle of Erzsébet Bridge on 4 July 2002, necessitating its being towed away.
On appeal, on 15 May 2003 the Buda Central District Court reduced the parking fine imposed on the applicant to 5,000 Hungarian forints.
On 16 June 2008 the applicant was convicted of 'disturbance of public works' within the meaning of section 260(1) of the Criminal Code.

The Government submitted that the ballot papers were bound for statutory destruction on 20 July 2002 as per section 5(3) of Decree no. 48/2001 (XII. 29.) BM on the Procedural Time-limits for the Legislative Elections of 7/21 April 2002.
In the applicant's view, the relevant law could be understood — and was by many — to the effect that the ballot papers could be destroyed as early as 7 July 2002.
On 2 July 2002, Parliament had decided not to put on the agenda a bill for the amendment of the 90-day statutory preservation period of the ballot papers.

The Pest Central District Court observed that the demonstration on 4 July 2002 had caused traffic to become paralysed all over Budapest for several hours.

The Budapest Regional Court noted that 'the message of the judgment is not that non-notified assemblies cannot be peaceful; the message is that an assembly, notified or non-notified, is not peaceful where, by its very manner, it constitutes unlawful conduct.'

The Budapest Regional Court referred to section 2(3) of Act no. III of 1989 on the Right of Assembly, according to which 'the exercise of the right of assembly may not constitute an offence, or instigation thereto, or violate the rights and freedoms of others'.

The Budapest Regional Court quoted the European Court of Human Rights' judgment in the case of Ezelin v. France (26 April 1991, Series A no. 202), establishing that 'in peaceful assemblies the protection provided under Article 11 of the Convention shall be ensured for the participants as long as they do not commit any reprehensible act on such an occasion'.

The Budapest Regional Court held that 'it directly follows from the case law of the Constitutional Court and the European Court of Human Rights that the peaceful or non-peaceful nature of an assembly does not depend on whether a participant broke or smashed an asset or applied violence against a property.'
The Budapest Regional Court held that an assembly may be rendered non-peaceful by passive conduct.

The Budapest Regional Court held that the accused parties' conduct, which in its outward appearance seemed to be peaceful, was rendered non-peaceful by its causal result — the major disturbance of road traffic — and was thereby not protected under the law.
